one_liner: Julia GPU ensemble ODE/SDE solvers that compile one trajectory per thread; against MPGOS (CUDA C++) results are mixed.
what_it_does: Solves many small, independent ODE or SDE problems (parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo, uncertainty quantification) on a GPU through the SciML ensemble interface: `solve(EnsembleProblem(prob; prob_func), GPUTsit5(), EnsembleGPUKernel(CUDA.CUDABackend()); trajectories = N)`, or the older array-vectorised `EnsembleGPUArray`. The user writes an out-of-place Julia right-hand side that returns an `SVector`. The lower-level `DiffEqGPU.vectorized_solve` / `vectorized_asolve` take a GPU array of prepared problems and return `(ts, us)` matrices that stay on the device. These are what the MPGOS comparison timed. It is not a library for one large ODE; for that, use OrdinaryDiffEq with a CuArray state.
how_it_is_fast: `EnsembleGPUKernel` generates one KernelAbstractions kernel (`ode_solve_kernel`, ndrange = number of trajectories) in which each GPU thread runs a complete integrator on its own problem: GPUTsit5 (FSAL, 6 RHS evaluations per step), GPUVern7/9, or Rosenbrock23, Rodas4/5P and Kvaerno3/5 for stiff problems. The state lives in StaticArrays, `@muladd` fuses multiply-adds, and Julia's GPU compiler inlines the user's RHS into the kernel. This removes the per-step kernel launches that make JAX or PyTorch vmap solvers slow. It is the same thread-per-system design MPGOS uses in CUDA C++, so against MPGOS there is no structural advantage: on the V100 at 8.4M trajectories the fixed-step time ratio (145.3 / 94.2 ms = 1.54) almost exactly matches Tsit5's 6 RHS evaluations per step over RK4's 4 (derived from page data).
when_to_use: 10^4 to 10^7 independent small non-stiff ODEs (a handful of states, Float32) on one GPU from Julia, e.g. parameter sweeps or Monte Carlo over u0/p.
You need per-trajectory adaptive stepping, callbacks or events, stiff integrators (Rodas5P, Kvaerno5) or SDE methods (GPUEM, GPUSIEA) inside the kernel.
Non-NVIDIA hardware: the same code targets CUDA, AMD ROCm, Intel oneAPI, Apple Metal and OpenCL backends, whereas MPGOS is CUDA-only.
Code already written against the SciML EnsembleProblem API, where switching from EnsembleThreads to EnsembleGPUKernel is a one-line change.
when_not_to_use: Maximum throughput on a datacenter NVIDIA GPU at very large ensembles: in the authors' own data MPGOS was faster on the V100 from 131,072 trajectories up (0.65x fixed step and 0.70x adaptive for Julia at 8.4M).
One large ODE whose cost is in a big structured f: use a CuArray state with OrdinaryDiffEq instead.

Short jobs where latency to the first result matters: Julia JIT compile time was excluded from every timing, and the high-level solve() transfers problems to the GPU and results back on every call (lower-level API tutorial).

Trajectories with very different costs (warp divergence; open issue #376), ContinuousCallback at high thread counts (out of dynamic GPU memory, open issue #219), SDEs with non-diagonal noise (open issue #331), or a RHS that needs generic linear algebra or allocations (#110).
Float64 on consumer GPUs: the docs recommend Float32, and only Float32 was benchmarked.

integration.dependencies: KernelAbstractions, SciMLBase, DiffEqBase, StaticArrays, Adapt, ForwardDiff, LinearSolve, SimpleDiffEq, SimpleNonlinearSolve and others; one GPU backend package loaded as a weak-dependency extension (CUDA.jl 6, AMDGPU.jl 2, oneAPI.jl 2, Metal.jl 1 or OpenCL.jl 0.10)
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat, DiffEqGPU 3.21.4); the MPGOS comparison used Julia 1.8.5 and DiffEqGPU 2.1.0
integration.platforms: NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm), Intel (oneAPI), Apple M-series (Metal), CPU via OpenCL/pocl
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the solver set replaces an MPGOS-style CUDA C++ ensemble solve, but the API is the Julia SciML EnsembleProblem interface, not MPGOS's ProblemSolver C++ class; RHS functions must be rewritten in Julia

gotchas: Crippled baseline (enricher finding, source-confirmed plus derived): GPU_ODE_MPGOS/Lorenz_SystemDefinition.cuh computes `10.0*( X[1]-X[0] )` and `X[0]*X[1] - 2.666 * X[2]` with double literals on float state, so every MPGOS RHS evaluation does FP64 multiplies and conversions; the Julia RHS uses 10.0f0 and 2.666f0. From the V100 to the RTX 5000, MPGOS slows 9.4x fixed step (94.157 to 886.082 ms at n=8,388,608) and 3.9x adaptive, while Julia slows only 1.27x and 1.20x (derived from page data). This is consistent with an FP64 bottleneck on the FP64-weak RTX 5000, so the RTX 5000 large-n wins (4.8x fixed, 2.3x adaptive) do not show faster code generation (inference; not rerun).

Where the baseline is not FP64-bound (V100, n of 131,072 or more), MPGOS wins, and the 1.54x fixed-step gap matches the 6-versus-4 RHS evaluation count of Tsit5 against RK4, so per-evaluation cost is a wash; the integrators were never matched (Tsit5 against RK4 and RKCK45).

Asymmetric timing: Lorenz.cu times one cold Solve() per process with clock() (process CPU time, which equals wall time only if the CPU spins during the synchronise), while bench_lorenz_gpu.jl reports the BenchmarkTools minimum of warm repeated `vectorized_solve` calls, with problem construction and the host-to-device copy outside the timed region. MPGOS's flat ~2 ms on the V100 for n up to 8192 produces the small-n 6-10x Julia lead.

Stale, fragile harness: data pin DiffEqGPU 2.1.0 and Julia 1.8.5 (current 3.21.4, which merged 'Reduce EnsembleGPUKernel CPU host overhead' #560 on 2026-10-04). run_ode_cpp.sh rewrites Lorenz.cu lines 15 and 17 with sed. MPGOS appends to ./data/cpp while run_benchmark.sh clears ./data/CPP, so repeated runs accumulate rows. MPGOS is built for sm_70 only, so the RTX 5000 ran JIT-compiled PTX.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl is the CPU sibling and the right choice for one ODE or a few hundred trajectories; pick DiffEqGPU when you have thousands to millions of small independent ODEs and a GPU, or need AMD/Intel/Apple GPU support that MPGOS (CUDA C++) lacks, but not on the strength of a speed win over MPGOS.
verified_claims_summary: First-party GPUODEBenchmarks data: Float32 Lorenz ensembles (8 to 8.4M trajectories, t in [0,1], dt 0.001, tolerances 1e-8) with DiffEqGPU 2.1.0 GPUTsit5 on Julia 1.8.5 against MPGOS RK4/RKCK45 built with nvcc -O3 for sm_70, on a Tesla V100 and an RTX 5000 (host CPU and CUDA version not stated). Julia was 6-10x faster for small ensembles on the V100 and 2.3-4.8x faster at 8.4M on the RTX 5000, but 0.65-0.70x as fast at 8.4M on the V100. The C++ side was timed cold once and its RHS is promoted to FP64.
status_note: Actively maintained (1,274 commits, Project.toml v3.21.4, newest commit 2026-10-08, 38 open issues) and MIT-licensed, so it is usable today. The MPGOS evidence is first-party and two major versions old, and its Julia wins trace to a cold-timed baseline (small n) and an FP64-promoted C++ RHS on an FP64-weak GPU (large n), so tier D under the crippled-baseline precedent is defensible.
